signals.excerpt:
Independent benchmarks show Qwen3.8 27B's 4-bit quantization (17 GB) matches the full 55 GB model on agentic coding tasks, while 1-bit compression (6.2 GB) collapses to random-chance performance on graduate-level science questions.

Illustration
...
A 17 GB four-bit quantization of Alibaba’s Qwen3.8 27B language model matches the full 55 GB BF16 version on an 89-task agentic coding benchmark, while compressing to one bit destroys performance to near-random levels on graduate-level science questions, according to a detailed evaluation published by Quesma on August 26.
...
The findings, authored by Piotr Migdał and posted on the Quesma blog, carry direct implications for agent developers deciding how aggressively to compress local models. The post reached the Hacker News front page on September 8, drawing 251 points and 124 comments.
...
Migdał tested five weight formats of Qwen3.8 27B, a 27-billion-parameter model released by Alibaba’s Qwen team in mid-August 2026. The GGUF quantizations were supplied by Unsloth on Hugging Face, with v2 files for the 2-, 4-, and 8-bit variants and v3 for the 1-bit builds.
...
- BF16 (full precision): ~55 GB
- Q8_0 (8-bit): ~29 GB
- Q4_K_M (4-bit): ~17 GB
- UD-Q2_K_XL (2-bit): ~10.7 GB
- UD-IQ1_S (1-bit): ~6.2 GB
...
All runs used llama.cpp with a build dated August 16, 2026, and F16 KV-cache at roughly 2.3 GB per 32k tokens of context, per the blog post. GPU time was rented from Modal, a cloud infrastructure provider, across NVIDIA L40S, H100, and H200 hardware. Migdał states the total cost was approximately $3,000.
...
Three benchmarks structured the evaluation: GPQA Diamond (graduate-level science), IFBench (instruction following), and Terminal-Bench 2.1 (agentic coding across 89 tasks). Each was run at three reasoning-effort settings: low, medium, and xhigh (the model default).
...
The headline result: Q4_K_M at 17 GB matched BF16 on Terminal-Bench 2.1, according to Migdał. On GPQA Diamond, the 4-bit model likewise showed “little difference” from the full-precision version, with deviations falling within Wilson 95% confidence intervals. The author replicated Qwen’s official reported scores on the first attempt, lending credibility to the test harness.
...
Two-bit compression (UD-Q2_K_XL, 10.7 GB) degraded results but remained functional. Coverage from MindPattern characterized the 2-bit penalty as roughly five points on agentic coding. Migdał described 2-bit as working “to some extent,” per the original post.
...
At one bit (UD-IQ1_S, 6.2 GB), the model collapsed. GPQA Diamond scores fell to approximately random chance, and higher reasoning effort made outcomes worse rather than better, according to the benchmarks. Migdał labeled the 1-bit variant “useless for these benchmarks.”
...

Migdał notes that the effort setting “matters a lot” and that the model can “overthink” at the default xhigh level — a phenomenon where extended chain-of-thought reasoning degrades rather than improves answers. At 1-bit precision, this overthinking effect is amplified: longer reasoning chains compound quantization errors, pushing accuracy below what a shorter, lower-effort pass would produce.
...
The practical takeaway centers on the RTX 4090, NVIDIA’s flagship consumer GPU with 24 GB of VRAM. The Q4_K_M build at 17 GB fits on a single 4090 with roughly 7 GB remaining — enough for approximately 64k tokens of context, per Migdał’s calculations. The full BF16 model at 55 GB requires multi-GPU or datacenter hardware.
...

The finding that 4-bit quantization preserves agentic coding performance while fitting on consumer hardware lowers the cost floor for deploying capable local agents. The 1-bit collapse, meanwhile, sets a hard boundary: ultra-aggressive compression eliminates the reasoning capacity that agentic workflows depend on. As agent orchestration frameworks increasingly support adjustable reasoning effort, understanding how quantization interacts with chain-of-thought depth becomes an infrastructure-level concern.

signals.title: DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash Brings 1M Context and FP4 KV Cache
signals.excerpt:
DeepSeek's new V4.1-Flash pushes a 1M-token context window with FP4 KV cache compression and cross-layer attention reuse, slashing memory costs for long-context inference and reshaping the efficiency frontier for large models.
...
DeepSeek AI has released DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, a long-context model that combines three aggressive efficiency techniques: a 1M-token context window, an FP4 KV cache, and cross-layer attention reuse. Taken together, these choices target the single biggest bottleneck in modern large-model serving — the memory and bandwidth cost of the key-value (KV) cache during long-context inference.
...
Every autoregressive transformer stores the keys and values for previously generated tokens so it doesn't have to recompute them at each step. As context windows stretch toward a million tokens, this cache balloons into the dominant consumer of GPU memory and the primary driver of latency. A model can have excellent raw FLOPS efficiency and still stall because the KV cache no longer fits in fast memory or because moving it around saturates memory bandwidth.
...
DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash attacks this on two fronts. First, it quantizes the KV cache down to FP4 — a 4-bit floating point representation — which roughly quarters the memory footprint compared to FP16 storage. Second, it introduces cross-layer attention reuse, sharing attention state across layers so the model doesn't need to maintain a fully independent cache for every transformer block. Both techniques compound: less memory per token and fewer distinct caches to store.
...
Dropping the KV cache to 4-bit precision is a delicate operation. Keys and values are highly sensitive to quantization error because attention scores are computed from dot products that amplify small deviations. The practical significance of a working FP4 KV cache is that it makes million-token contexts economically feasible on commodity hardware, rather than requiring exotic memory configurations. For workloads that ingest entire codebases, long documents, transcripts, or multi-hour media logs, this changes the cost calculus dramatically.
...
Cross-layer attention reuse is part of a broader research trend — including grouped-query attention and multi-head latent attention — aimed at reducing the number of independent KV tensors a model must hold. By letting multiple layers draw on shared attention representations, DeepSeek reduces both the storage and the compute redundancy of stacking many attention layers. The tradeoff is always representational: sharing too aggressively can degrade quality. The interesting engineering claim in a Flash-class release is that the quality loss is minimal enough to be worth the efficiency gains for high-throughput serving.
...
DeepSeek has built its reputation on aggressive efficiency engineering, and V4.1-Flash continues that pattern. The FP4 KV cache and cross-layer reuse are the kinds of systems-level optimizations that separate a model that can support a 1M context on paper from one that can serve it affordably at scale. As the industry converges on ever-longer contexts, the winners will increasingly be decided not by parameter counts but by how cheaply they can move and store attention state.
